html:
Amartya Sen is an Indian economist and philosopher who won the Nobel Prize in economics in 1998. His work changed how the world understands famine and measures poverty.

He was born in 1933 at Santiniketan in Bengal, on the campus of the school founded by Tagore, who chose his name. At nine he watched starving people walk into the town during the Bengal famine of 1943. He studied in Calcutta and Cambridge and has taught at Delhi, Oxford and Harvard.

His book Poverty and Famines, published in 1981, studied that famine and others. Bengal, he showed, had no less food in 1943 than in earlier years. People starved because wartime prices rose beyond what labourers, fishermen and barbers could pay. Famine is a failure of people's means to get food, not of supply. He added that no large famine has happened in a working democracy with a free press, since rulers who face voters must act.

He also argued that a country should be judged by what its people are able to do and be: to live long, read, stay healthy and take part. The United Nations' Human Development Index of 1990 puts this into figures.

In 1990 he reckoned that 100 million women were "missing" in Asia because girls received less food and care.
